title: I Turned My E30 BMW into a Riot on Wheels

body_markdown:
In early 2015, I was searching the Canadian classifieds site Kijiji for a Datsun 240Z, a Porsche 911 G, or an old 3 Series BMW. I had a modest budget and wanted something as original as possible. I ended up responding to an ad by a guy about an hour from me. His name was Tony, and he worked at a Mercedes dealership that had taken a[1987 325e](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/bmw-e30-3-series-buyers-guide/) on a trade-in in the mid-1990s; he purchased it for his wife to drive. She had recently parked the car behind a Sears and a delivery truck backed into it, which slightly dented the hood. Tony decided it was time to sell, and I saw the hood as an excuse to add a carbon fiber one…


We agreed on a price and soon[the BMW was in my driveway](https://www.instagram.com/wap_trap) —an all-original E30 coupe in Bronzit Beige Metallic with a four-speed automatic and power windows. It even came with the new-car limited warranty records, all booklets, service history, and more.


I drove it for about 16 months before my curiosity and perfectionism overpowered me. This led to a complete teardown in my garage with one goal: to build a better car than any manufacturer could sell me.


Arthur Jaworski


Arthur Jaworski


With the exception of the car’s fully custom stainless exhaust, I did all the work myself. First and foremost was an engine swap. Out went the original 2.7-liter straight-six and automatic, and in went the 4.4-liter M62 V-8 and six-speed manual I pulled out of a ’97 E39 540i.


I’ve always loved the grumble of big motors, but I tried to remain mindful of the E30’s geometry and structural integrity during the swap. The M62 seemed like the biggest engine I could comfortably fit, without having to cut or repurpose the bay too much.


There were a handful of barriers but none seemed impossible, especially because I was in no hurry. There are a few well-documented solutions for mounting the M62 in an E30, but I disagreed with cutting the oil pan to clear the subframe. I also wanted to use OEM motor mounts, so I took the time to design subframe spacers in AutoCAD and machined them myself out of stainless steel. As a result, the motor sits exactly how it would in an E39 engine bay. I made the drawings available via forums, and it generated a small income that helped complete the project.


I did have to do some hammering to the transmission tunnel and a little cutting to fit the alternator, but it was all reasonable. I also found sources stating that the M62 is actually lighter than the car’s original M20B27 due to the cast aluminum vs. forged steel makeup. I reasoned that if I set the new motor farther back in the engine bay, the heavier transmission would improve the car’s center of gravity. The geometry checked out, and I got my V-8 rumble.


Arthur Jaworski


Arthur Jaworski


My E30 came with the standard “diving board” front bumper, which stuck out so far it was really all you’d see from the side profile. My favorite front end of that era is the Mtech2 style, with the bumper tucked in, so I paired the valance from a late-model E30 with a custom fiberglass bumper that is tucked so far inward I had to modify the turn signal housing to make it work. But it gives the front end a look far sleeker than any OEM front bumper, in my opinion.


One of my favorite aspects of the car is the paint. I made a booth in my garage and used high-quality automotive paint to make my E30 Tanzanite Blue Metallic with Diamond Silver in the engine bay.


Arthur Jaworski


My patience with this project certainly paid off. When I finally stood over the car and listened to it run for the first time in five years, all I could think about were the memes of project cars sitting on jack stands indefinitely. But not this one. My E30 BMW has been a riot ever since it got to see the light outside the garage again!


Outside of car shows and track days, I love taking my custom E30 on casual outings. It certainly drives like no other car.
